The combination of dataset generation, forecasting, transfer to experimental data, and PDE evaluation is potentially significant. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/c137716763884b6bab0165be44af2745/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed dataset is unusually large for nonlinear-dynamics research, and the attempt to select candidate systems using several chaoticity and stability tests is more principled than unrestricted equation randomization.

Panda incorporates sensible inductive biases, particularly alternating temporal and channel attention. The ablations provide evidence that multichannel modeling improves performance, and the coupling-strength experiment is a useful qualitative test of this hypothesis.

The evaluation spans thousands of synthetic held-out systems, three experimental datasets, two discretized PDEs, multiple forecast horizons, and several error metrics. The paper is visually polished and generally well organized.
weaknesses: The held-out evaluation does not convincingly establish generalization to genuinely new dynamics. Training and test systems are mutations and skew-product recombinations of the same small collection of 135 curated families. Although 20 founders are held out, test skew products may still contain a training founder as their other component, and no quantitative analysis establishes dynamical or topological separation between the splits. Consequently, the reported 9,300-system sample size may substantially overstate the effective diversity of the test set.

Baseline coverage and implementation details are insufficient for the central forecasting claim. The paper compares mainly against generic time-series foundation models, but omits strong dynamics-specific zero-shot or locally fitted methods such as autoregression, analog forecasting, DMD/Koopman methods, reservoir computing, and next-generation reservoir computing. Context lengths, normalization, channel handling, deterministic versus probabilistic decoding, hyperparameter selection, and comparable fine-tuning budgets are not documented well enough to judge fairness.

The real-world evidence is limited to three datasets and appears to use very few underlying trajectories. Sample counts, train/test window construction, preprocessing, statistical uncertainty, and robustness across recordings or subjects are not reported. The coupling experiment compares only against Chronos-SFT and therefore does not isolate channel attention from other architectural differences.

The PDE claim is substantially stronger than the evidence. Only two PDE instances are tested, with little information about preprocessing, spatial encoding, normalization, channel ordering, evaluation windows, or independent simulation seeds. Since a discretized PDE is itself a coupled ODE system, this result is interesting transfer rather than evidence of a qualitatively emergent PDE capability. Comparisons to simple dynamics baselines and appropriate zero-shot or pretrained operator models are also absent.

The claimed scaling law is based on eight nested dataset subsets apparently trained once each. There are no model-training seed replicates, uncertainty over the fitted exponent, alternative functional-form comparisons, or evaluation on independently generated system families. Error bars over many correlated forecast windows cannot substitute for variation across training runs, so the result currently supports a diversity trend rather than a neural scaling law.

The interpretability and nonlinear-resonance conclusions are speculative. Structured attention maps and entropy responses to two-tone inputs do not demonstrate physical resonance, gain, or a causal forecasting mechanism. Essential controls such as randomly initialized models, shuffled channels, alternative patch sizes, frequency/phase perturbations, and non-attention response measures are missing; patching and aliasing alone could produce lattice structure.

Appendix E contains a technical error in its correlation-dimension calculation. From C(r) proportional to r^D2, the small-distance density scales as r^(D2-1); this is not equivalent to fitting a Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha) for r greater than rmin, nor does it imply D2 approximately equals alpha. Thus Figure 17 does not validate preservation of attractor dimension as claimed.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a contribution whose main asset is a generated dataset. Important mutation scales, selection thresholds, recombination details, acceptance rates, optimizer and learning-rate settings, normalization procedures, split identifiers, and dataset/code availability are missing. Overall, the ideas and preliminary results are promising, but unresolved split validity, baseline fairness, statistical support, and overclaimed mechanistic interpretations keep the work below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The synthetic-data direction is interesting: constructing a large collection of chaotic ODEs and studying whether dynamical diversity improves transfer could be valuable to scientific machine learning.

Panda combines temporal and channel attention with nonlinear patch features in a sensible architecture that can accept varying numbers of variables, and the channel-attention ablation provides some evidence for multivariate modeling.

The empirical scope is broader than a single synthetic benchmark, covering thousands of held-out systems, three experimental datasets, two PDE examples, multiple forecast horizons, and several error metrics.
Holding the number of training timepoints fixed while varying the number of systems is a useful first experiment for separating dynamical diversity from raw dataset size.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly support the paper's strongest claims. Comparisons are primarily against general-purpose time-series models; there are no competitive dynamics-specific, neural-operator, reservoir-computing, or system-identification baselines, nor trained-from-scratch controls that separate the architecture, synthetic pretraining, and test-time context effects.

The real-data evidence is limited to three datasets and the PDE claim to two cases. Dataset sizes, evaluation windows, preprocessing, normalization, missing-data handling, and uncertainty across trajectories or runs are insufficiently documented. The PDE comparison also omits specialist PDE forecasting models, making the claimed spontaneous PDE capability substantially overstated.

The purported discovery of 20,000 novel chaotic systems is weakly validated. The systems are largely parameter perturbations and skew-product recombinations of 135 known systems, while the paper provides no quantitative analysis of duplicate or near-duplicate attractors, topological diversity, false-positive rates of its chaos tests, or novelty relative to the founders. The description also does not substantiate the framing as a genuine evolutionary search.

The held-out protocol does not establish transfer to wholly unrelated equation families: test systems are mutations and skew products generated by the same procedure as training, and a test skew product may contain a component derived from a non-held-out founder. Additional splits by functional form and comparisons against much simpler interpolation or nearest-founder baselines are needed.

The scaling-law conclusion is based on nested dataset subsets and apparently one training run per setting. Consequently, system identity is confounded with system count, optimization variance is unmeasured, and the reported test-set error bars do not establish a reproducible neural scaling law.

The interpretability claims are speculative. Visual structure and entropy in attention rollouts do not demonstrate nonlinear resonance, causal use of those patterns, or a mechanism responsible for forecasting performance. Frequency-matched controls, output-response measurements, interventions, and layer/head-level ablations are missing.

The appendix's correlation-dimension derivation is technically questionable: fitting a Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha) over the 5th-to-50th percentile of pairwise distances is not equivalent to estimating the small-radius relation C(r) proportional to r^(D2), and D2 is not generally equal to the stated Pareto exponent. This undermines the quantitative completion analysis.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a large empirical contribution. Important information such as optimizer and learning-rate schedule, mutation and augmentation parameters, feature allocations, normalization and inference procedures, baseline tuning, training variability, compute time, and availability of equations, data, and code is absent. Overall, the paper contains promising ideas and visually favorable results, but major evaluation, validation, and claim-calibration gaps make it uncompetitive in its current form.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and potentially impactful direction: pretraining a general forecasting model on a large, procedurally generated collection of chaotic dynamical systems.

The synthetic-data pipeline is a substantive contribution. It combines mutation, skew-product recombination, and several chaoticity filters to expand a small set of curated systems into roughly 20,000 training systems.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: evaluation covers approximately 9,300 held-out synthetic systems, three experimental datasets, two chaotic PDEs, several forecast horizons, and multiple error metrics.

Panda consistently outperforms relevant time-series foundation-model baselines, including a Chronos model fine-tuned on the same synthetic corpus. Its strong transfer to experimental data and PDEs is particularly promising.

The architecture is well motivated by the application. Interleaved temporal and channel attention is appropriate for coupled dynamics, and the ablations provide evidence that multivariate channel modeling materially improves performance.

The diversity-scaling experiment is insightful because it holds the number of training observations fixed while varying the number of distinct systems, offering useful evidence that dynamical diversity matters independently of raw dataset size.
The manuscript is engaging, generally clear, and connects modern time-series modeling with ideas from nonlinear dynamics and Koopman-inspired representations.
weaknesses: The external validation is narrower than the paper's broad universality claims suggest. It uses only three experimental datasets and two PDE configurations, and the manuscript does not clearly report the number of independent trajectories, evaluation windows, or statistical tests for these results.

The PDE comparison includes only general-purpose time-series baselines. Comparisons with pretrained neural operators, reservoir-computing methods, or other PDE/dynamics-specific models would better establish the significance of the claimed emergent PDE capability, even if those methods require in-domain training.

The held-out synthetic systems are numerous but highly related: they are mutations and recombinations derived from a small founder collection. Treating thousands of related descendants as independent evaluation units may overstate both dataset diversity and statistical confidence. Stronger family-level or structurally dissimilar holdouts are needed.

The scaling-law claim is based on eight nested dataset subsets and apparently one training run per setting. Error bars seem to reflect evaluation variation rather than training-run uncertainty, so the fitted power law and exponent are not yet robustly established.

The attention analysis is suggestive rather than mechanistic. Lattice patterns in attention-rollout entropy are described as nonlinear resonance largely by visual analogy; random-weight, shuffled-channel, frequency-resolution, and alternative-architecture controls are needed to rule out generic attention or sampling artifacts.

The appendix's correlation-dimension derivation appears incorrect: the small-distance distribution associated with a correlation dimension does not generally have the stated tail form p(r) proportional to r^{-alpha}, and the conclusion D2 approximately equals the fitted alpha does not follow. This weakens the completion analysis, although it is not central to the forecasting results.

Reproducibility information is incomplete for a contribution of this scale. Important details such as optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, normalization and preprocessing, precise augmentation distributions, random seeds, repeated-run variability, and a concrete code/data release plan are missing.

Some architectural conclusions are internally mixed: the dynamics embedding hurts performance when combined with masked pretraining, and masked pretraining degrades rollout performance. The final model-selection rule and the contribution of each proposed component should be stated more precisely.

Overall, the paper has concrete evidence of a competitive and meaningful contribution, but several claims—especially universality, neural scaling, and interpretability—are stronger than the current experiments support. These issues keep it near the acceptance boundary rather than at a clear accept score.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem: zero-shot forecasting of unseen chaotic dynamical systems. Its combination of synthetic pretraining, multivariate attention, and dynamics-inspired representations is well motivated.

The evolutionary data-generation pipeline is a substantial contribution. The authors construct roughly 20,000 training systems, apply several chaos and stationarity filters, and use a founder-level split intended to prevent direct descendant leakage.

The empirical study is broad: 9,300 held-out synthetic systems, several forecast horizons and metrics, architecture ablations, probabilistic and supervised-fine-tuned baselines, experimental time series, two PDE examples, inference-time measurements, and model/data scaling experiments.

PANDA obtains consistent and often sizable improvements over general-purpose time-series foundation models. The ODE-to-PDE transfer and generalization from three-channel training to many-channel inference are particularly interesting observations.
The manuscript is generally clear, candidly reports regression-to-the-mean and rollout degradation, and provides many implementation details and additional results in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main synthetic test set uses the same skew-product construction, normalization, integration protocol, and filtering pipeline as training. Holding out founder systems is useful, but does not establish generalization beyond this narrow generator family; test systems may also retain a familiar parent subsystem. Consequently, the description of 20,000 'novel' systems and broad universal-dynamics claims are stronger than the evidence.

The baseline set is dominated by general-purpose univariate foundation models. It omits important dynamics-specific or simple adaptive references such as DMD/linear autoregression, reservoir computing or next-generation reservoir computing, SINDy-style approaches, and PatchTST or other multivariate models trained under comparable data and compute. Thus it is unclear how much of the gain comes from pretraining, multivariate modeling, or simply using a better-matched forecasting architecture.

Evidence on genuinely external systems is limited to three experimental datasets and two PDE trajectories/settings. Numerical tables, dataset sizes, independent runs, and uncertainty definitions are not adequately reported for these experiments. The PDE comparison also lacks specialist neural-operator or dynamics baselines, making the claimed emergent PDE capability promising but not yet convincing.

The long-term-geometry claim is overstated. Forecasts regress toward the mean beyond the trained 128-step horizon, while KL and spectral metrics compare relatively short predicted segments with much longer trajectories and do not include estimator uncertainty or a ground-truth finite-sample reference. Low distributional error under these metrics does not by itself demonstrate preservation of attractor geometry.

The proposed correlation-dimension calculation appears technically questionable: fitting pairwise distances with a tail density proportional to r^{-alpha} and identifying the resulting tail exponent directly with the Grassberger-Procaccia dimension is not generally equivalent to estimating the small-radius slope of log C(r). This weakens the completion and dataset analyses that rely on this estimator.

The reported 'scaling law' is based on single nested dataset subsets and apparently one training run per setting. It simultaneously changes the number of systems and initial conditions and provides no variability across training seeds, so the power-law interpretation is more descriptive than established.

Several design claims are not cleanly supported by the ablations: the dynamics embedding can hurt short-horizon performance, MLM pretraining hurts rollout, and multiple components change together. Code/data links are blank in the submitted PDF, limiting reproducibility despite the useful hyperparameter details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: transferable forecasting of chaotic dynamics using large-scale synthetic pretraining.
The family-level split, which excludes held-out founder systems and their descendants from training, is more meaningful than a simple trajectory-level split.

The synthetic evaluation is large, reports multiple pointwise and distributional metrics, and includes statistical tests, architectural ablations, efficiency measurements, and qualitative failure cases.
The cross-channel transformer is well motivated for coupled dynamics, and the results consistently show gains over the evaluated univariate time-series foundation models.
weaknesses: The principal claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. The alleged 20,000 'novel' systems are mostly parameter perturbations and skew-product combinations of 129 curated systems. Their correlation dimension is essentially unchanged from that of the founders, suggesting limited growth in dynamical complexity. Moreover, the stated additive coupling is undefined when the two parent vector fields have different dimensions, which the paper says range from 3 to 10; the missing construction details create a technical and reproducibility concern.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. Comparisons focus on generic, predominantly univariate time-series foundation models. The paper lacks strong dynamical-system baselines such as reservoir computing, state-space approaches, local linear/autoregressive methods, neural ODE or operator models, and a comparably trained multivariate PatchTST-style model. Consequently, the results do not establish that Panda is competitive with appropriate methods for chaotic forecasting or that its gains arise from the claimed innovations.

The real-data evidence is narrow and poorly documented: only three datasets are shown, primarily against Chronos-SFT, without clear sample counts, uncertainty estimates, numerical tables, or comparisons with domain-specific and simple classical baselines. This is insufficient to support broad real-world generalization claims.

The 'emergent PDE forecasting' claim rests on only two PDE examples, apparently one simulated trajectory per system, with no evaluation across initial conditions or physical parameters. The von Karman experiment additionally uses PCA computed on the simulated data without clarifying whether the basis or normalization accesses the evaluation interval. Generic univariate forecasting models are weak controls, so these experiments do not convincingly demonstrate PDE-level transfer.

The claimed scaling law is based on eight nested dataset configurations and apparently one training run per configuration. Error bars reflect evaluation systems rather than training variability, while the number of systems is confounded with the number of initial conditions per system. A fitted curve with high R-squared is therefore not sufficient evidence for a robust neural scaling law.

The long-term-statistics claim is overstated. Evaluation extends only to 512 steps, the paper acknowledges regression to the mean beyond the 128-step training horizon, and prediction-only Lyapunov statistics are in several cases worse than Chronos-SFT. Comparing short predictions against the distribution of a 4096-step trajectory also requires much more precise estimator and sensitivity analysis.

Several theoretical motivations are imprecise. Random coordinate-specific delays and rectangular convex or affine projections are not automatically diffeomorphisms by Takens' theorem, and random polynomial/Fourier features are described as a dynamic-mode embedding without demonstrating a Koopman or DMD property. The attention-map 'nonlinear resonance' interpretation is likewise speculative and unsupported by causal controls.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central dataset contribution: the code and dataset footnotes are blank, and important details such as mutation variance, selection thresholds, dimensional reconciliation during recombination, preprocessing of experimental data, random seeds, and complete PDE evaluation protocols are missing.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful contribution: a procedurally generated dataset of roughly 20,000 chaotic ODE systems together with a pretrained multivariate forecasting model specialized for nonlinear dynamics.

The zero-shot evaluation on approximately 9,300 held-out systems is unusually large. PANDA consistently improves over several pretrained time-series models across pointwise, spectral, and distributional metrics, with statistical tests and uncertainty summaries.

The model incorporates sensible dynamical-system inductive biases, particularly cross-channel attention, and the ablations provide evidence that multivariate coupling is important. The inference-speed advantage over Chronos is also practically relevant.

Generalization is evaluated beyond synthetic held-out systems on three experimental datasets and two PDE benchmarks. The ODE-to-PDE transfer result is especially interesting and suggests that the learned representations capture reusable dynamical structure.

The study of training-set diversity while holding the number of timepoints fixed is well motivated and provides compelling empirical evidence that increasing the number of distinct systems improves out-of-domain forecasting.

The paper is ambitious, clearly organized, and unusually thorough in its appendices, including numerical integration details, additional metrics, failure cases, patch-size studies, scaling experiments, and compute information.
weaknesses: The baseline set is dominated by general-purpose univariate time-series foundation models, which are structurally disadvantaged on coupled multivariate dynamics. Comparisons against strong dynamics-specific alternatives such as reservoir computing, nonlinear autoregression, DMD/Koopman methods, state-space models, or locally fitted numerical predictors are missing. This limits the claim that PANDA is broadly competitive for chaotic forecasting.

The main synthetic test set remains closely matched to the training distribution: both are produced by the same mutation, skew-product recombination, filtering, normalization, and timescale-standardization pipeline. Holding out founder systems and descendants is valuable, but does not establish generalization across substantially different equation-generation mechanisms.

The external evidence is promising but narrow. Results cover only three experimental datasets and two PDEs, apparently at limited parameter settings, without comparisons to dynamics-specialized or PDE-specialized zero-shot approaches. Thus, the strong characterization of PDE forecasting as an emergent general capability is not yet fully supported.

Some long-term-geometry claims are overstated. PANDA is acknowledged to regress toward the mean beyond its training horizon, and prediction-only Lyapunov-exponent correlations are sometimes worse than Chronos-SFT. Metrics computed after concatenating predictions with the context can also be dominated by the ground-truth context.

The correlation-dimension procedure used for completion evaluation is questionable: it applies a Pareto-tail MLE over the 5th-to-50th percentile of pairwise distances and identifies the fitted exponent directly with correlation dimension, whereas correlation dimension is conventionally obtained from the small-radius slope of log C(r) versus log r. This analysis requires stronger justification or validation.

The proposed components do not all receive clean empirical support: the dynamics embedding hurts performance when combined with MLM at the trained horizon, MLM degrades rollout performance, and smaller patches outperform the default at short horizons. These results weaken the architectural narrative, even though channel attention is convincingly supported.

The diversity scaling experiment appears to use nested datasets and single training runs; its error bars primarily reflect test examples rather than training variability. Multiple independently sampled datasets and random seeds would be needed to establish a robust scaling law. The larger-model results are additionally confounded by simultaneous changes in model size, training duration, dataset size, initial conditions, and timescale diversity.

Reproducibility is only partial: many implementation and integration details are supplied, but the manuscript does not provide an accessible code/data link in its current form, and reproducing the full dataset-generation and training pipeline requires substantial specialized compute.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem: zero-shot forecasting across unseen chaotic dynamical systems. Its synthetic-data strategy, based on mutation, skew-product recombination, numerical integration, and chaos filtering, is creative and potentially useful beyond this specific model.

The empirical study is unusually broad. It covers 9.3k held-out systems, multiple forecasting horizons and metrics, several pretrained time-series baselines, real experimental data, long-rollout statistics, architectural ablations, computational efficiency, and two PDE examples.

Panda achieves convincing short-horizon improvements over strong transformer baselines, including Chronos fine-tuned on the same synthetic dataset. The reported MAE improvements are substantial, and the large test set plus paired significance tests provide reasonably strong evidence for the central forecasting result.

The channel-attention architecture is well motivated for coupled dynamics, and the ablations generally support its importance. The diversity-scaling experiment is also an interesting result, suggesting that coverage of distinct systems matters more than repeatedly sampling initial conditions from fewer systems.

The paper is clearly written, visually polished, and candid about several limitations, including mean regression at long horizons, interactions between masked pretraining and rollout quality, and the imperfect comparability of recurrent and operator-learning baselines.
weaknesses: The claimed out-of-domain generalization is narrower than the framing suggests. Most test systems are generated by the same mutation, recombination, filtering, normalization, and integration pipeline as the training systems, from only 20 held-out founders. This establishes family-level compositional transfer, but not broad generalization to arbitrary unseen dynamics. Evaluation on the original held-out founders and on substantially different equation-generation mechanisms should be reported quantitatively.

The PDE evidence is not sufficiently controlled to support the strong claim of an emergent PDE forecasting capability. Only two PDE datasets are tested, and the FNO and DeepONet comparisons use one-step models trained and rolled out under acknowledgedly non-comparable conditions. For the vortex data, evaluation also consists of a single trajectory split into only four windows. Comparisons with competitive pretrained PDE models, reservoir methods, persistence/linear autoregression, and properly trained in-domain neural operators are needed.

The real-data evaluation is limited to three datasets and is presented mainly through curves without numerical tables, uncertainty estimates, sample counts, or significance tests. This makes it difficult to judge robustness across trajectories, preprocessing choices, and forecast starting points.

The proposed architecture is largely a combination of established components—patching, axial temporal/channel attention, random Fourier and polynomial features, and masked pretraining. The ablations show that channel attention helps, but support for the dynamics embedding and masked objective is mixed and horizon-dependent, weakening the architectural novelty claim.

The attention analyses are overinterpreted. Structured entropy maps and attention patterns do not by themselves demonstrate nonlinear resonance, recurrence-based computation, Fourier-like transforms, or mechanistic interpretability. Stronger controls and causal interventions on specific heads or features would be required.

The advertised scaling law is based on eight nested dataset subsets and apparently one training run per setting. It lacks uncertainty across independently sampled datasets and optimization seeds, and the fitted functional form is not compared with plausible alternatives. It is better viewed as a promising diversity trend than an established neural scaling law.

Long-term claims require qualification: Panda becomes worse than Chronos-SFT and DynaMix on KL divergence at longer horizons under both the paper's primary estimator and the alternative estimator, and its tail forecasts exhibit severe mean regression. The headline statement about preserving distributional measures therefore holds only for selected metrics and horizons.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted artifact: code, weights, and dataset links are blank, while several consequential details of the attractor-selection thresholds and evaluation preprocessing are not fully specified. If this is solely anonymization, functional anonymous resources would still materially strengthen verification.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and challenging problem: zero-shot forecasting across nonlinear dynamical systems rather than fitting a separate model to each system.
The synthetic-data pipeline is ambitious, and the ancestry-based separation of training and test founders is more careful than a simple trajectory-level split.

The proposed model combines patching, temporal attention, and channel attention in a sensible way. The paper includes architectural ablations, parameter scaling experiments, efficiency measurements, and evaluations over thousands of synthetic systems.

The authors report multiple pointwise and distributional metrics and candidly document important failure modes, including mean regression and cases where competing methods perform better at long horizons.
weaknesses: The central out-of-domain claim is insufficiently established. Test systems are produced by the same parameter-perturbation and skew-product construction used for training. Holding out founder systems prevents direct leakage, but does not demonstrate generalization beyond this narrow equation-generation grammar.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed method's value. Most baselines are generic univariate foundation models, while DynaMix is evaluated with a short context that the paper acknowledges disadvantages it. Strong classical and learned dynamics baselines—such as reservoir computing/NVAR, autoregressive models, local analog methods, and appropriately trained multivariate forecasters—are missing.

The PDE evidence does not support the strong claim of an emergent PDE forecasting capability. Only two PDEs are tested, and FNO and DeepONet are trained as one-step models and then rolled out, whereas Panda receives a 512-step history and directly predicts blocks. The paper itself concedes that these baselines are not directly comparable. This setup cannot establish superiority over PDE-specific methods.

The real-world evaluation is small and weakly documented: it covers only three datasets, primarily compares against Chronos-SFT, and provides plots without sufficiently detailed aggregate statistics, uncertainty, sample counts, or preprocessing protocols. The circuit coupling analysis may be confounded by coupling-dependent changes in the underlying dynamics and does not directly ablate channel attention on these data.

The correlation-dimension procedure appears mathematically incorrect. From C(r) proportional to r^D, the small-distance density scales as r^(D-1), not r^(-alpha); consequently, identifying the Pareto MLE exponent alpha with the correlation dimension is unjustified. Using the 5th–50th distance percentiles and apparently no Theiler window further conflicts with standard estimation for temporally correlated trajectories. This undermines the completion results and parts of the dataset analysis.

The long-horizon conclusions are selectively positive. Panda becomes worse than Chronos-SFT and DynaMix under the alternative geometric-misalignment KL estimator, and its tail-only metrics are substantially worse because of mean regression. The sensitivity of conclusions to the KL estimator is not resolved.

The claimed scaling law is based on nested dataset subsets with no clear independent training replicates or uncertainty over runs. A high-quality fit to eight correlated points is descriptive evidence of a diversity trend, but is insufficient to establish a neural scaling law.

The interpretability claims are speculative. Structured attention-entropy maps do not by themselves demonstrate nonlinear resonance, recurrence computation, or Fourier-like operations, and the univariate control does not rule out architectural artifacts.

Architectural novelty is moderate, and the dynamics-specific embedding has inconsistent ablation results, sometimes hurting performance. The experiments do not cleanly separate gains from multivariate attention, synthetic-data scale, and the proposed embedding.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the reproducibility statement contains blank code and checkpoint links, and the generated dataset and exact evaluation pipeline are not made available in the manuscript. Statistical testing also emphasizes extremely small p-values from a large, hierarchically related test set without addressing dependence among descendants or reporting matched effect sizes.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and potentially impactful contribution by combining a scalable procedure for generating approximately 20,000 chaotic ODE systems with a dynamics-oriented pretrained forecasting model.

The primary synthetic evaluation is unusually broad: Panda is tested on roughly 9,300 held-out systems descended only from held-out founder equations, across several forecast horizons and pointwise, spectral, geometric, and invariant-dynamics metrics.

Results are consistently strong against several pretrained time-series models, including a Chronos model fine-tuned on the same data. The reported gains in MAE are substantial, statistically significant, and accompanied by an approximately 60-fold inference-speed advantage over Chronos-20M.

The architecture is well motivated by the domain. In particular, alternating temporal and channel attention is appropriate for coupled dynamics, and the corresponding ablation provides concrete evidence that multivariate modeling matters.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond aggregate forecasting accuracy: controlled dataset-diversity scaling, real experimental signals, long rollouts, model and data scaling, patch-size studies, qualitative failure cases, and extensive implementation details.

Zero-shot transfer from low-dimensional ODE training to experimental data and discretized PDE trajectories is compelling evidence that the learned representation captures some reusable dynamical structure.
weaknesses: The PDE comparison does not adequately support the strongest headline claim. The FNO and DeepONet baselines are trained as one-step predictors with very little PDE-specific data and then rolled out, an acknowledged disadvantage relative to Panda's 512-point context and 128-point output. Stronger PDE models, matched training budgets, and direct comparisons to persistence, autoregressive, or context-conditioned operator baselines are needed.

The empirical baseline suite is dominated by univariate general-purpose time-series foundation models. The DynaMix comparison uses a short-context setting unfavorable to that recurrent model, and the study lacks competitive multivariate forecasting or reservoir-computing baselines trained on the same generated corpus. Thus, the gains cannot yet be cleanly attributed to Panda's particular architecture rather than multivariate supervision and favorable task matching.

The real-world validation is narrow—three datasets—and is presented mostly through plots without sufficiently clear sample counts, uncertainty, statistical tests, and preprocessing/evaluation protocols. This limits confidence in the claimed robustness to noise, missingness, and nonstationarity.

The claimed 'scaling law' is based on a single nested sequence of dataset subsets, apparently without independent training seeds. Consequently, subset composition and optimization variance are confounded with system diversity, and the fitted power law should be viewed as preliminary evidence of a trend rather than an established law.

Several interpretability claims are overstated. Structured attention-entropy responses to two-tone inputs do not by themselves demonstrate learned nonlinear resonance, and attention-map patterns are not sufficient evidence for specific internal operations such as recurrence analysis or Fourier transforms.

Long-horizon conclusions are metric-sensitive. Panda becomes worse than Chronos-SFT and DynaMix on very long-horizon KL divergence, performs substantially worse under the alternative geometric-misalignment KL estimator, and exhibits severe mean regression in tail-only evaluation.

The completion analysis appears technically questionable: fitting a Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^{-alpha} over truncated pairwise distances and identifying alpha with the Grassberger–Procaccia correlation dimension is not generally equivalent to estimating the slope of log C(r) versus log r. This weakens the auxiliary claim that masked completions preserve fractal dimension.
